prompt: What are the common mistakes with pattern matching in Java and how can they be avoided?
completion:
## Pattern Matching in Java – What goes wrong most often (and how to stop it)

Pattern matching is one of the newest “syntactic sugar” features that came to Java in JDK 16/17 (JEP 394, JEP 406).  
It lets you:

| Feature | When it became stable | Typical use |
|---------|-----------------------|-------------|
| **`instanceof` pattern** | JDK 16 | `if (obj instanceof String s) { … }` |
| **Type and record patterns in `switch`** | JDK 17 | `switch (obj) { case Integer i -> …; case Person p -> …; }` |
| **Record patterns** | JDK 17 | `case Person(String name, int age) -> …` |
| **Sealed‑class exhaustiveness** | JDK 17 | `switch (sealedObj) { case SubA a -> …; case SubB b -> …; }` |

Once you have the syntax under your belt, the **real pitfalls** are often **semantic**—mixing old patterns with the new, ignoring scope rules, missing exhaustive cases, etc.

Below is a consolidated list of the *most common mistakes* that developers run into, why they happen, and how to avoid them. I’ll sprinkle in short code snippets so you can see the “bad” vs. the “good” in a single glance.

---

### 1. **Using the wrong Java version or preview flag**

| ❌ Bad | ✅ Good |
|-------|--------|
| Compile on JDK 15 and write `instanceof String s` | Compile on JDK 17+ **or** compile with `--enable-preview` on an earlier JDK |
| Forget to add `--enable-preview` when using JDK 16 preview | Pass the flag or upgrade to a stable release |

> **Why it fails** – The compiler simply doesn’t recognize the new syntax.  
> **Fix** – Always target Java 17 or newer, or explicitly enable preview features.

---

### 2. **Syntax mix‑ups and “illegal variable name” errors**

| ❌ Bad | ✅ Good |
|-------|--------|
| `if (obj instanceof String s)` – *no* parentheses, *no* `var` keyword | `if (obj instanceof String s)` is correct syntax; adding `var` is illegal |
| `if (obj instanceof String string)` – variable name collides with existing local variable | Rename the pattern variable (`String s`) or remove the existing one |
| `switch (obj) { case Integer i -> i * 2; case String s -> s.length(); }` – missing `default` in a *switch expression* when type is sealed | Add `default` or cover all subclasses |
| `case MyRecord(int x)` – `MyRecord` is not a record | Define `record MyRecord(int x);` or use correct class name |

> **Why it fails** – Pattern variables follow the same rules as any Java variable.  
> **Fix** – Use distinct names, ensure the target type is a record if you use a record pattern, and add a `default` if the compiler complains about exhaustiveness.

---

### 3. **Scope and “effectively final” rules**

| ❌ Bad | ✅ Good |
|-------|--------|
| `if (obj instanceof String s) { System.out.println(s); } s = "foo";` | Keep `s` usage **inside** the `if` block. If you need a mutable copy, assign it to a new variable. |
| `case Person p -> { System.out.println(p); p = null; }` | `p` is implicitly `final`; you cannot reassign it. Use a separate variable if needed. |

> **Why it fails** – Pattern variables are *effectively final* and scoped to the `if`, `while`, or `switch` block in which they appear.  
> **Fix** – Treat them as read‑only, and if you need to mutate a value, copy it to a new variable.

---

### 4. **Misunderstanding that patterns are *only* compile‑time**

| ❌ Bad | ✅ Good |
|-------|--------|
| Expecting a runtime type check that “optimizes” away casts | Pattern matching simply replaces a manual cast with a concise syntax. It doesn’t change the runtime behavior beyond a standard cast. |

> **Why it fails** – Some people think patterns give a “shortcut” that avoids any check. In reality, the JVM still does the type check the same way it would for a cast.  
> **Fix** – Use patterns for *readability*, not performance.

---

### 5. **Forgetting the `default` case in a switch expression**

| ❌ Bad | ✅ Good |
|-------|--------|
| `switch (obj) { case Integer i -> i * 2; case String s -> s.length(); }` – no default → compile error in Java 17 | `switch (obj) { case Integer i -> i * 2; case String s -> s.length(); default -> 0; }` |

> **Why it fails** – Switch expressions *must* return a value for every possible input. If the type is *sealed* or *non‑enum*, the compiler will enforce exhaustiveness.  
> **Fix** – Either add a `default` branch or ensure you handle *all* subclasses.

---

### 6. **Using pattern matching with generics incorrectly**

| ❌ Bad | ✅ Good |
|-------|--------|
| `if (obj instanceof List<String> list)` – not allowed (type erasure) | `if (obj instanceof List<?> list)` or helper method that checks element type |
| `switch (obj) { case List<String> l -> … }` – illegal | `switch (obj) { case List<?> l -> … }` |

> **Why it fails** – Java erases generic type parameters at runtime. `instanceof` can’t check the generic arguments.  
> **Fix** – Use raw types or runtime checks on the elements, or use helper methods like `isListOfString(Object o)`.

---

### 7. **Attempting to match primitive types**

| ❌ Bad | ✅ Good |
|-------|--------|
| `if (obj instanceof int i)` – compile error | Use wrapper class `Integer` or cast manually `if (obj instanceof Integer i)` |

> **Why it fails** – Pattern matching works only with reference types.  
> **Fix** – Wrap primitives in their wrapper classes before pattern matching.

---

### 8. **Misusing record patterns**

| ❌ Bad | ✅ Good |
|-------|--------|
| `case Person(String name, int age) -> …` – but `Person` is a normal class | Use a `record Person(String name, int age)` or a normal class with a pattern that matches its fields (`case Person p -> …`) |
| `case Person(String name, int age) -> …` – wrong number of components | Match exactly the number of components defined in the record |

> **Why it fails** – Record patterns deconstruct *records* only.  
> **Fix** – Declare your type as a record, and supply the exact component list.

---

### 9. **Using patterns with arrays or unsupported types**

| ❌ Bad | ✅ Good |
|-------|--------|
| `if (obj instanceof int[] arr)` – compile error | `if (obj instanceof int[] arr)` is *actually* allowed in Java 17; but `switch` cannot match array types. Use `instanceof` only, or cast manually. |
| `case String[] arr -> …` in a switch expression – compile error | Use `if (obj instanceof String[] arr)` instead of a switch case. |

> **Why it fails** – Switch pattern matching currently supports only reference types that are *class*, *enum*, or *record* (and *sealed* classes). Arrays are not supported in switch patterns.  
> **Fix** – Use an `if` chain for array checks.

---

### 10. **Mixing old and new style casting**

| ❌ Bad | ✅ Good |
|-------|--------|
| ```java
   if (obj instanceof String) {
       String s = (String) obj;
       …
   }
   ``` | ```java
   if (obj instanceof String s) {
       …
   }
   ``` |

> **Why it fails** – The old style is still valid, but the new style is shorter and less error‑prone. Mixing both can lead to duplicate casts or confusion.  
> **Fix** – Prefer the new pattern syntax; remove the explicit cast.

---

### 11. **Misunderstanding the `yield` keyword in switch expressions**

| ❌ Bad | ✅ Good |
|-------|--------|
| ```java
   switch (obj) {
       case Integer i -> {
           System.out.println(i);
       }
   }
   ``` | ```java
   int result = switch (obj) {
       case Integer i -> i * 2;
   };
   ``` |
| ```java
   case Integer i -> { i * 2; }
   ``` | ```java
   case Integer i -> { yield i * 2; }
   ``` |

> **Why it fails** – In a *switch expression*, the branch must produce a value. If you write a block (`{ … }`) you must `yield` that value.  
> **Fix** – Either use the expression form (`case Integer i -> i * 2;`) or add `yield`.

---

### 12. **Ignoring the *sealed* class exhaustiveness**

| ❌ Bad | ✅ Good |
|-------|--------|
| `switch (sealedObj) { case SubA a -> …; case SubB b -> …; }` – new subclass added but not covered | `switch (sealedObj) { case SubA a -> …; case SubB b -> …; default -> …; }` or update the switch to cover the new subclass. |

> **Why it fails** – Sealed classes provide a *fixed* set of subclasses. The compiler can enforce that all cases are handled. If a new subclass appears, you’ll get a compile‑time error.  
> **Fix** – Keep the switch up‑to‑date or add a default case that throws.

---

### 13. **Over‑using pattern matching where it adds complexity**

| ❌ Bad | ✅ Good |
|-------|--------|
| Multiple nested `instanceof`/`switch` to deconstruct a deep type hierarchy | Use a single `switch` expression or a guard clause, or extract the logic into a helper method |

> **Why it fails** – Too many patterns can become a readability nightmare.  
> **Fix** – Keep patterns simple; use helper methods or extract logic.

---

## How to Avoid These Mistakes – A Checklist

| ✅ Item | What to do | Quick tip |
|--------|------------|-----------|
| **Target the right JDK** | Compile with Java 17+ or enable preview (`--enable-preview`). | `javac --release 17` or `--enable-preview` |
| **Use IDE support** | Modern IDEs (IntelliJ, Eclipse) auto‑complete pattern syntax and warn about missing `default`. | Enable the *Java 17+* language level. |
| **Keep pattern variables final** | Don’t reassign; treat them as read‑only. | If you need to change, copy to a new variable. |
| **Add `default` or handle all sealed subclasses** | Switch expressions must be exhaustive. | For sealed types, use a `default` that throws or returns a sentinel. |
| **Do not use generics in patterns** | Use `?` or helper methods for type‑erased checks. | `instanceof List<?> list` |
| **Record patterns only for records** | Verify the class is declared as `record`. | `record Person(String name, int age)` |
| **Avoid primitives** | Wrap in `Integer`, `Double`, etc. | `if (obj instanceof Integer i)` |
| **Don’t mix old and new casts** | Prefer the new syntax. | `if (obj instanceof String s)` |
| **Remember `yield` in block switch expressions** | Either use the expression form or `yield`. | `case Integer i -> { yield i * 2; }` |
| **Test exhaustive switches** | Unit‑test with all subclasses. | `assertTrue(switch(obj) { … } == expected);` |
| **Use `instanceof` only for reference types** | No arrays, primitives, or type arguments. | `instanceof List<?> list` |

---

## Quick “Bad vs. Good” Cheatsheet

```java
// 1. Wrong: Java 15, no preview
if (o instanceof String s) { … }

// 2. Wrong: shadowing variable name
String s = "x";
if (o instanceof String s) { … }   // error: duplicate variable

// 3. Wrong: reassigning pattern variable
if (o instanceof String s) { s = "y"; }   // error: cannot assign to final

// 4. Wrong: no default in sealed switch
sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square {}
switch (shape) {
  case Circle c -> …
  case Square s -> …
}   // compile error: switch is not exhaustive

// 5. Wrong: record pattern on non‑record
case Person(String name, int age) -> …   // Person is a class, not a record

// 6. Wrong: using generics in pattern
if (o instanceof List<String> list) { … }   // not allowed

// 7. Wrong: using primitive in pattern
if (o instanceof int i) { … }   // not allowed

// 8. Wrong: missing yield in block
int n = switch (obj) {
  case Integer i -> { i * 2; }   // error
  default -> 0;
};

// 9. Wrong: pattern in switch but missing null case
switch (obj) {
  case String s -> …
}   // null will fall through and cause exception

// 10. Good
if (o instanceof String s) {
    System.out.println(s);
}

sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square {}
switch (shape) {
    case Circle c -> …
    case Square s -> …
    // no default needed because sealed and exhaustive
}

record Person(String name, int age) {}
switch (obj) {
    case Person(String name, int age) -> …
    default -> …
}

int n = switch (obj) {
    case Integer i -> i * 2;
    case String s -> s.length();
    default -> 0;
};
```

---

## Final Take‑aways

1. **Pattern matching is *syntactic* sugar, not a runtime magic** – it’s just a cleaner way to write `instanceof` + cast.
2. **Scope matters** – pattern variables are `final` and local to the `if`/`switch` block.
3. **Exhaustiveness is enforced** – especially with sealed classes; missing a subclass will surface as a compile‑time error.
4. **Generics and primitives are out of scope** for patterns – stick to reference types.
5. **Switch expressions need `yield` or an expression** – blocks must return a value.
6. **Upgrade or enable preview** – you can’t use the syntax on an old JDK without the flag.

Once you keep these rules in mind, pattern matching becomes a *powerful* way to write concise, type‑safe code. Happy coding!
